entry.title: Four Ways I’d Solve the Clothes Chair
entry.summary: Including a wall-mounted drying rack and a patchwork pouf to camouflage laundry.
entry.content:
Clothes chairs are an inevitability, much like death and taxes: Nobody wants one, but everyone ends up with one anyway — Bernie Sanders included. At its most essential, the chair is a rest stop on the way from the closet to the laundry bin, holding clothes that aren’t clean but aren’t really dirty (a state described as “clurty” by one of our respondents). From that toehold, the clothes chair takes on additional roles: dumping ground for fresh laundry, staging area for tomorrow’s clothes, a semipermanent holding area for garments without a clear home.

If the chair is universal, so is the fantasy of eliminating it — everyone I talked to for this article wanted it gone. But I’d argue that the clothes chair cannot be organized away; remove it and piles will emerge in its place. It performs an essential function, and if we accept that clurty clothes are part of life, we can treat them like part of a system rather than clutter. Below are four solutions to four very different clothes-chair quandaries. To find previous installments of “Clutter Clinic,” click here — and if you have a mess for me to fix, email a photo and a brief explanation to strategist@nymag.com.

Primary complaint: “I have a FreshDirect bag full of sweaters on the floor next to my dresser that are in that liminal space where you have definitely worn them but they are not yet dirty. I don’t want to hang them up or put them in a drawer.”

I am with you here — sweaters do not like being hung up (gravity puts stress on the fibers), and they take up a lot of space in a dresser. This corner is cramped at ground level but has plenty of space if you build upward. Why not add a bookcase just for sweaters? This accomplishes a couple of things — a case will contain the sweaters on three sides, keeping them from sliding around, and it will give you more storage space vertically. The sweaters are happy, the pile is gone, and you don’t have to hang them.

The cheapest option here would be a dinky medium-density fiberboard shelf from Wayfair, but next to your dresser, I feel you deserve real wood. Search for “unfinished wood furniture” in your area — I found these two shelves at Gothic Furniture, which has locations in Manhattan and Queens. They can be stained to match the dresser, or you can save money by handling the finish yourself (or leaving them unfinished). I’ve also included a similar shelf from Lowe’s that ships for free.

Facebook Marketplace and AuctionNinja are also essential stops; you can’t beat the quality-to-price ratio of secondhand wooden furniture. I love the carved details on this skinny shelf, and for more options, search “bookcase” and filter for location here.

Primary complaint: “I would love to not have a clothes chair because it’s visually unappealing but have never in my life been able to figure out a different solution. Sometimes I put my favorite clean clothes on there because I’m like, I’m gonna wear these ASAP. I want it to look more intentional, less like a person has died and evaporated there.”

This is such a pretty corner, and I believe we can sneak some clothes storage in here without abutting the closet door or making it look like someone melted. The plant is already anchoring this area, and more bulk on the floor cuts into your walking path — I’d suggest moving the entire clothes chair up, mounting a wall rack that can hold a few items and display tomorrow’s clothes.

One option is a dowel rack, which can be expanded or collapsed flat depending on what it’s holding. I’ve included a collapsible Amish-made wall dryer and two options from Etsy, one with lower and higher capacity. (If you don’t mind lower capacity, I also love this metal one from the former USSR.)

I also found this handmade walnut shelf from a furniture store in Ukraine, which has a towel bar you could drape a pair of jeans over and a shelf above for stacks of clothes. The dimensions shown aren’t quite right for the asker’s space, but the seller offers custom sizes via DM.

Primary complaint: “I pile my clothes everywhere, and I wear what’s on top of the piles. There’s a valet chair from Ikea with stuff hanging off it, a pile of clothes I mainly wear around the house, and a bag of sweaters that need dry cleaning. Almost everything in this photo is “clurty” (not clean but not dirty). I need to do a purge of things I don’t use anymore, keep up with the dry cleaning, and find places to put the clean clothes. Looking at it makes me feel gross!”

The challenge here is congestion — the clothes aren’t making it back to their homes, so the piles grow. I agree that donating unworn things is a good first step (if you’re in New York, try St. Mary’s Clothing Drive — you can schedule a pickup online, and it’s free). Then start putting everything away, but change the goal: Let yourself off the hook for clearing the piles today. Instead, tune into your reactions, notice where you feel stress and friction. Take those feelings seriously — write them down.

Maybe you hate looking for something in a dark closet or the feeling of forcing a drawer shut or not being able to see an important garment. Maybe there is not enough space to store everything. Then reset your space based on what you’ve learned about what makes you feel good. The key to organization is not self-discipline, it’s self-love; approach the piles with curiosity and they’ll take another shape.

Light has been really helpful for me, so I’ve linked a set of motion-activated stick-on LEDs above. Some other ideas: an atomic-style coat rack to keep the house clothes accessible, vacuum bags for storing clothes you don’t wear, under-bed boxes for less-worn clothes (I think of this as having an A team and a B team), very skinny clothes hangers to maximize closet space, and a wall-mounted pot rack you could use as a hanger for smaller garments or accessories.

Primary complaint: “I hate displaying any form of laundry in the open. I want a solution that hides the clothes so my chair can just be a chair.”

The clothes stick out on a spindly wooden chair, but I wonder if they would look less prominent against a textile. I found two ottomans that would do the trick, one made of denim, cotton, and linen and the other made of woolens (tartan and tweed) — the patchwork will camouflage the mix of fabrics.

If the goal is to hide the laundry, a mirror is as close to a disappearing act as you can get. There are three options below: an Ikea mirror with a clothing rack behind it that we spotted on Maryam Nassir Zadeh’s Instagram and two versions from Wayfair that rotate 360 degrees — one that hides a rack and shelving, the other with a full cabinet behind it.

entry.title: On My Mind: Redecorating Two Tween Bedrooms at Once
entry.summary: Plus eyeball jewelry and puffer-coat shoes.
entry.content:
Every room in my house is in some sort of flux. My daughters are 8 and 11 now, and figuring out how different spaces need to evolve as they get older has become something of an all-consuming logic puzzle. We live in the suburbs and have the luxury of multiple bedrooms, but until a few months ago, the girls shared one anyway; in July, we moved the 11-year-old into what we previously called the guest room but had kind of become a dumping ground for whatever didn’t fit elsewhere (we don’t actually host many guests). At one point I had grand plans of picking her up from a week of summer camp — which ended right before her birthday, with middle school on the horizon — and surprising her with a flashy home-makeover-show reveal. But in reality it’s been a series of half-measures, whatever we can get done and afford little by little. Finding good stuff on Facebook Marketplace and then going to pick it up takes time. And of course she has so many of her own ideas, as does her younger sister.

Untangling the two kids’ stuff has been tough. I obviously should have anticipated more of the arguments over what belongs to whom, and who gets to keep what, since peak sibling rivalry was one of the reasons for making the split in the first place. It’s like going through a breakup. One girl is happily still sleeping in the twin-size bunk bed they previously shared, surrounded by a bunch of books and toys that need sorting though and clearing out. The other is starfishing in the expanse of a queen-size bed that came with the place and peppering us with questions about when we’re going to get the rest of our own junk out of there, repaint, and put up shelves. Each has an ever-changing wish list full of new furniture and décor and will inevitably be getting bedding and home goods for Christmas. Parents who’ve done this before: Please, share your wisdom!

One of the first things we bought to help personalize the new room fast was this cat switch plate to zhuzh up an outlet that’s in a particularly visible and inconvenient spot.

Even though she now has an entire closet to herself, the 8-year-old has become obsessed with getting a locker like the one her sister has at school. We’ve been browsing Mustard Made because the colors are so good; she likes the double-wide Twinny in light pink, which will probably be easier and more versatile to organize inside, though I also see the appeal of side-by-side Skinnys in different colors. (Thankfully the brand has a sale is coming up.)

When my older daughter was an infant and we lived in a one-bedroom apartment, I bought an an oversize Miffy lamp that was cheaper a decade ago but a splurge nonetheless. We plunked it down on mine and my husband’s dresser, then newly cleared off to make room for a changing pad on top, and used it during nighttime feedings and diaper changes. It’s been around ever since, a softly glowing bunny beacon who these days always has necklaces and headbands looped around her ears. Neither girl wants to part with it, so the older one has requested this smaller version.

This cheerful yellow — and actually affordable — coat rack might be handy for the child whose wardrobe is 90 percent hoodies.

Both kids need new desks for doing homework, drawing, and crafting. They also both need bookshelves, storage for art supplies, and a place to display their favorite LEGO builds, squishies, and assorted mementos and trinkets. I’m all over the place between simple tables combined with modular drawers, desks that have built-in drawers and hutches, wall-mounted systems that will make better use of vertical space, sit-to-stand desks that will literally grow with them, neutrals versus bright colors, and trying to stick to a budget while also wanting to avoid particleboard and having regrettably expensive taste. (It doesn’t help that the closest Ikea is two hours away.)

The older kid needs a comfy place to lounge and read. I think she would absolutely lose it if we got her a papasan chair, but they’re kind of gigantic. I also think it’d be awesome to have a hanging chair or cocoon swing in one corner, but the layout of the room doesn’t allow for that and I’d like to be able to easily move it around. So I’m still on the hunt.

I am simply unable to resist an eye motif and will be adding these Grainne Morton studs to my Christmas list once I decide between a matching pair or singles in different colors.

My sister’s got a milestone birthday coming up, and I am currently hyperfixated on buying two of these incredible Emma Brooke googly eye charms for us to wear as BFF tokens. They com in sterling silver or 14-karat gold and really move!

I am attempting to DIY a squishy dumpling Halloween costume to wear when I volunteer for one daughter’s classroom party next week. Assuming one of these inflatable “body bumpers” will fit me, it could make a good base.

I previously had a tortiseshell case from Flaunt on my iPhone and loved the look of the squared corners until they started a hole in the back pocket of a beloved pair of jeans. Now I’m testing this case from Urban Sophistication that seems very appropriate for the change in seasons. It’s sadly not MagSafe compatible, but it is pretty comfortable to hold.

I tend to go full puff as soon as it gets even slightly cold, so these slip-ons are looking especially plush right now.

entry.title: I Know Which iPad You Should Get
entry.summary: I’ve tried nine models since 2012, including all the models in the current lineup.
entry.content:
Since the first iPad was released in 2010, Apple has come out with 45 models of its tablet, including versions of the iPad Air, Mini, and Pro. At least one product in the lineup changes every year, and it can be hard to figure out which one works best for your needs. Apple currently sells four iPad models, two of which come in two sizes. iPads with faster processors will be better for heavy tasks like video editing and will have better longevity than those with slower or older chips. But if you don’t plan on using an iPad as your main work device, you might consider a cheaper model with a screen that’s almost as good as the one on pricier models.

I’ve been using iPads since 2012 for taking notes in school, serving as my primary nonwork computer, and doing illustrations for my newsletter, among many other tasks. I’ve chosen different models depending on my changing needs and in that time have learned what the best-use cases for each iPad in Apple’s lineup are. Whether you’re an illustrator, photographer, or just a casual reader who likes a big, bright screen, there’s an iPad for you.

Update on October 21, 2026
Updated to the most recent models; updated prices and checked stock for all products.

The iPad Air, Apple’s mid-range tablet, has a powerful chip that can run all the apps most people use to get work done, plus its display and thin design make it an excellent tablet for watching videos and reading. It also has support for Apple’s Pencil, Pencil Pro, and Magic Keyboard, all of which expand the tablet’s capabilities to more robust illustration work and writing (Apple’s keyboard case is good enough for replying to all your emails, too).

The Air has a 10.9-inch display that’s just a tad smaller than the (smaller) 11-inch iPad Pro, but the difference is barely noticeable. Its display doesn’t have quite as fast a refresh rate, which is what makes things like video playback and scrolling look significantly better on the Pro, but you’ll only miss the feature if you’ve spent a lot of time with it. For everyday use, the iPad Air still makes videos look good.

On the other hand, the maximum storage for the Air is 1TB, while the Pro goes up to 2TB. Additionally, because it uses the previous-generation M4 chip, the Air isn’t quite as powerful as the Pro, with its M5 processor, but the difference likely won’t be noticeable unless you do a lot of resource-intensive work on your tablet (things like working on video projects with a lot of clips will take longer on a less powerful chip). Having an older processor does mean that the Air will probably stop being supported before the Pro, but Apple has a good track record of keeping older devices updated for at least a few years.

Apple also sells a 13-inch version of the Air that’s identical in all but size. Given its extra weight and larger footprint, it doesn’t work quite as well for in-hand usage, but the larger screen is better for taking notes, drawing, and editing photos.

My biggest gripe with the Air is that it doesn’t use FaceID for unlocking and security (only the high-end iPad Pro supports FaceID). Instead, it uses an older TouchID sensor, which works well but is not as convenient or as fast since you have to hold your finger on the unlock button for a second for it to work.

The top-of-the-line iPad is great as a laptop replacement or as a more powerful tool for heavy video and image work. The latest model is equipped with Apple’s M5 chip, and the company’s most powerful tablet to date. That won’t make a difference for things like checking email or working in Google Docs, but the extra power will come in handy if you’re using this as your daily driver, and the Pro will get updates for longer than the Air given its newer processor.

The 11-inch model is slightly larger and wider than the Air, but it’s not enough of a difference to be a dealbreaker, and both weigh about a pound. Compared to the Air, the Pro’s display has slightly higher resolution, double the brightness, and double the refresh rate (and on the top-end models, you get the option of a nano-texture surface). That makes the Pro superior for editing videos and doing illustration work: the screen feels more responsive when you’re drawing with a stylus, but even just for watching movies and browsing the web, this display looks better.

Like the Air, the Pro supports both the Apple Pencil and the Pencil Pro and the Magic Keyboard, though the latest Pro models have an updated keyboard with an aluminum palm rest. These accessories are quite pricey, and these iPads start at well over $1,000 already, at which point you could also consider buying a MacBook. The newer M5 processor will provide more longevity than the Air’s M4 chip, but even so, there are similarly priced MacBooks that can do more simply because the professional app ecosystem is more mature, and Mac apps can access more system utilities than iOS permits. You can also connect more external displays to a MacBook than an iPad, which may make a difference depending on your office setup.

If none of that matters and you want the most powerful iPad that’ll work for years to come, get the iPad Pro. The 11-inch model’s screen is a bit small for illustration work, though I’ve been able to make it work just fine. On the other hand, it’s portable and light, so it’s easy to hold when you just want to read or play a game, and even with the Magic Keyboard attached, your bag won’t feel too heavy with it in tow.

If you take a lot of notes or doodle a lot on your iPad, get the 13-inch iPad Pro. It gives you significantly more real estate for using the Apple Pencil (plus about a quarter pound more weight). I had an older version of this size Pro, and I still miss the extra space when I’m drawing in ProCreate, even though its extra heft is significant. My hands got tired much faster when I held the 12.9-inch model for more than 20 or 30 minutes, and with the Magic Keyboard attached, it’s heavy enough to make you question whether you should just have a laptop instead. Paired with a lightweight case, though, this iPad can’t be beat for artists and students who like to take notes by hand.

No iPad is more portable than the iPad Mini. It has an 8.3-inch screen that’s packed into a body you can hold with one hand. It’s not quite compact enough to compete with a Kindle, but it’s still small enough to work as a travel reader and has many more capabilities beyond that. It’s by far the lightest iPad, and feels nice to hold — it’s my favorite tablet to use on the couch.

Like all other current iPads, the Mini works with the Apple Pencil, including the Pencil Pro. Unfortunately, it’s one of the only iPads Apple sells that doesn’t have an M-series chip, so it’s significantly slower than most other models. That won’t matter for things like reading and web browsing, which is really what this tablet is best for, but since Apple only refreshes this line every few years, you’ll have to compromise on processing power for portability. And like the Air, this tablet uses TouchID for security instead of FaceID.

According to Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang, “the best iPad to get a kid is a hand-me-down.” But if you don’t have an extra tablet laying around, Apple’s entry-level iPad is a perfectly fine tablet that’s notably cheaper than the other models. That’s mostly because it runs on a much slower chip, in this case the A16, and Apple’s A-series processors aren’t anywhere near as powerful as the M-series — it’s really best for light tasks like watching YouTube videos and playing games like Minecraft.

There are a few other compromises. Its screen doesn’t have an anti-reflective coating like all of the other iPads, for one thing. And the keyboard case for this iPad just isn’t as good as the one for the Air or Pro. Unlike the Magic Keyboard, which uses a laptop-like hinge to adjust the iPad’s viewing angle, the Magic Keyboard Folio for the iPad uses an adjustable stand on the back of the case. You can’t use it on your lap as easily as you can the Magic Keyboard, since it doesn’t have one solid base, but it works fine on a flat surface.

entry.title: A Gift for Every Type of Girlfriend
entry.summary: From splurges to “just because” pick-me-ups.
entry.content:
I like to think of myself as a professional girlfriend. I held the title for ten years before becoming a wife, and to this day, I believe that my excellent gift-giving abilities had something to do with keeping us happy and in love all those years. My strategy is simple: Pay attention and be specific. Did she recently decide to join a cookbook club? Easy, another cookbook or cooking-adjacent accessory like a sheet pan. Does she go on about how much she loathes the “big light” in her office? Amazing, get her a nice-looking lamp. The key here is to customize things to her taste and listen for the little things. But I get that that can be easier said than done, so I’ve compiled gifts based on what girlfriends (yours included) could like, broken down into very specific things she might be into like Ultrafragola mirrors or traveling or gold grills.

To make your search even easier, all the gifts on this list are available on Amazon. (For those who like to shop around, we’ve included links to other retailers when a gift is available elsewhere). entry.title: I’m on the Boatneck Boat
entry.summary: It’s my new neckline of choice.
entry.content:
I became a certified boatneck truther over the summer after buying two (now unfortunately mostly sold-out) tees during a really good sale at Kotn. And perhaps it’s confirmation bias, but it feels like the neckline is everywhere right now. It’s a classic transitional-weather piece for fall: Obviously, you don’t want to bundle up with a turtleneck just yet, but it’s getting a bit too cold to be exposing your entire neck in a scoop-neck situation. The boatneck hits that perfect mix of a little sexy (exposed collarbone) and a little structured (see every marine top). Plus it’s a good excuse to wear a bra with cute straps.

The Goodwill gods really blessed me with this find last winter. Now I love it so much that I need to buy a few more colors full price. I own it in the ivory shade, which I use for all kinds of layering. It looks nice with a tank top or tee layered on top — a method that also shows off my tattoos a little. During chilly weather, I like to wear is as a whisper-thin (but surprisingly warm!) layer under a sweater. I always wash in a lingerie bag and air-dry it, and it’s held up very well with minimal pilling. It’s very stretchy; mine is an extra large, but I could easily size down to a large or even a medium.

Purveyor of fine sergercore attire Baserange obviously makes a nice boatneck. I purchased mine on sale at END. in hen yellow, which the brand no longer makes. It’s a bit revealing on its own, so if I decided to repurchase it, I would probably opt for black. While the fabric is fairly stretchy, I did have to size up a little to an extra large. Fair warning that the sleeves are extremely long (which is usually my preference).

After my dabbling with long-sleeve boatnecks, this was the tee that actually cemented my dedication to the cause. I own it in the blue-on-blue stripe pictured here as well as solid black. Normally, I like the neckline to be a little less dramatic; it often slips off one shoulder, which actually makes me feel very character in a mid-century film set in the French Riviera. The fabric has some stretch and is incredibly soft — par for the course for Kotn. And the banded hem ensures everything sits nicely and doesn’t expose my midriff too much.

It seems to be sold out in most colors and sizes, but sign up for the wait list; hopefully, it won’t be too long before the company brings it back! In the meantime, this tee from Gap is similar.

This Best in Class long-sleeve is nearly always on sale. It is quite stretchy and falls “between light- and mid-weight,” says creative strategist Carrie Carrollo, but the fabric still “feels substantial.” There was a point in time when she was wearing it weekly, and after every wash, it seemed “to only be getting softer.”

And I’m loving the sleeve length on this inexpensive tee from Gap Factory.

An option with a pocket, straight from the Strategist Fall 100.

A lot of alt-celebs — think Clairo, Audrey Hobert, Zoë Kravitz, Phoebe Bridgers — own this tee from Cleo. Writer Kitty Guo is also a fan: “It’s made out of a comfortable fine-rib cotton that sits close to the skin for a flattering, body-skimming silhouette with quarter-length sleeves perfect for showing off your bracelets,” she says. Writer Kat Gillespie also recently joined the camp: “I got this because the reversible nature of it really tickled me and I am always looking for a top that can be worn both day and night,” she says. “It’s the perfect top to wear when you don’t know what to wear. The other night I wore it to see David Byrne at Forest Hills, then attend my friend’s ‘bisexual awareness party’ in Bushwick afterwards.”

As our senior writer Liza Corsillo says, this splurgy option from Flore Flore is “the kind of T-shirt I imagine rich people have in multiples but I save for the days I want to look rich.” And the neckline “shows off a totally appropriate amount of clavicle,” she adds.

For a three-quarter-length sleeve that’s a fraction of the price, this one from Kotn fits the bill.

A little ruching at the waist takes the silhouette of this boatneck up a notch.

Same theory here, though the shorter sleeves make it better for date night.

It’s never too early to buy next year’s summer boatneck, especially when it comes recommended by two Strategist staffers.

Deputy editor Simone Kitchens liked the aforementioned tank top so much that she immediately purchased this version too. Ava Dunn, who manages a prop-rental studio in New York City, told us the baby-rib fabric is super soft and flattering. “It looks good on everyone,” she says. “I’ve convinced many friends to join me in owning every color.”

My two current obsessions — boatnecks and pointelle fabric — rolled into one.

I’ve yet to venture into the world of boatneck cardigans. Once I do, this grape number is at the top of my wish list.

Oddli’s dual-buttoned tops and dresses have been courting me for months.

The bell sleeves on this boatneck dress are a nice touch.

Rat Boi’s polka-dot mini also speaks to me — and would look lovely with colorful tights.

entry.title: I Tried on All the Men’s Sweaters at J.Crew
entry.summary: And there’s a new great rollneck in town.
entry.content:
Long before skinny suits and barn jackets, J.Crew was known for its stylish, competitively priced knitwear. The venerable mall brand’s sweaters reliably offer better designs and more color choices than more affordable brands, while matching the construction and material quality one would expect from a blue-chip designer. I was reminded of this earlier this week, when I visited the J.Crew Men’s Shop in Noho to try every single sweater in the store.

I pulled 15 options over my head and each felt well made from high-quality materials — some even had an extra tag indicating the yarn’s origin, like the DOP seal on a fancy cheese or olive oil. A few sweaters were meant to be baggier, others were more tailored, but you can trust the designers to determine the right proportions for every silhouette. I am a true size medium in most tops, and I had no fit issues with any of the medium sweaters I tried. Overall, a handful of designs felt slightly more compelling than the rest, but I’d happily wear any of them again — with one minor exception.

For a brand so well known for rollnecks and cashmere, you’d think a cashmere rollneck would be a no-brainer, but it’s been about a decade since J.Crew last offered one in its men’s line. Having tried it on, I struggle to understand why it waited so long. Like the classic 1988 rollneck, it has a curled collar, hem, and cuffs, but they’re rendered more subtly in heavyweight cashmere. Where the cotton original is proudly oversize and slouchy, the softer cashmere version is more fitted and versatile. It’s relaxed enough to pull over a collared shirt, yet slim enough to fit under a suit jacket or chore coat, and it looks just as good with stonewashed jeans as it does with a blazer and trousers.

In recent years, J.Crew’s heritage cotton crewneck has had a more casual raglan sleeve, but I prefer the more elevated look of the new version’s standard shoulder seams. I originally tried the medium but liked the large a bit better. The heavyweight cotton knit drapes so luxuriously; why not get a bit more for your money?

Let’s be honest, how often is it actually cold enough to wear a heavyweight wool sweater in New York? This new soft-washed sweater still has the shaggy texture, variegated coloring, and elegant drape of a classic Shetland sweater, but it’s much lighter and more breathable. It’s soft enough to wear over a T-shirt and has a wide neck opening that layers easily over a collared shirt. While the sweater itself is made in China, it is knit from Yorkshire-spun yarns.

The waffle knit of this raglan-sleeve cashmere sweater gives it a slinkier drape and a smoother, cooler texture for incredible next-to-skin comfort. It wears more like a long-sleeve tee than a typical cashmere sweater and moves exceptionally well. The cut is pretty tailored, with just enough room to layer over a button-up shirt, but the texture is so nice that I can’t imagine you’d ever want to do that.

This subtly cropped sweater combines the smooth cotton neck of a rugby polo with the warmth and reassuring drape of a heavyweight wool knit body. It’s thick enough that you won’t need a topcoat on most fall days, and it would pair well with light-wash jeans or carpenter pants.

This chunky Aran-style fisherman’s sweater from J.Crew’s heritage workwear line, Wallace & Barnes, is knit from genuine Irish Donegal yarns. Its vibrant emerald hue and chunky texture look even prettier in person. Sadly, it’s already sold out online, but you may still find it in stores.

Cotton gets you that chunky sweater look without the sweat-inducing heat retention of thick lambswool. It also takes dye more readily, so designers can achieve deeply saturated colors that really pop. This butter-pink cable-knit sweater has a yellow undertone that’s hard to see in photos but is really noticeable in person.

J.Crew’s reissue of this iconic sweater coincided with burgeoning ’90s nostalgia and the release of Hulu’s Love Story to create a rollneck renaissance that led even rollnecks from other brands to sell out for months on end. The hype has only recently settled down as supply has finally caught up with demand. With scarcity out of the picture, is this thing really worth it? I like the oversize fit, drapey material, and low price. But a sweater like this demands to be the centerpiece of any outfit it’s a part of. I bought one last year and haven’t worn it as much as I thought I would because it’s hard to layer.

J.Crew’s cashmere crewneck sweater has been one of the best values in fashion since it was introduced in the 1980s. It’s just thick enough to layer over a button-down shirt without looking lumpy, yet light enough to not feel stifling at an overheated New York house party in the dead of winter. It has a more elegant drape and drier texture than cheaper sweaters because it’s knit from finer Grade A fibers, which are more consistent and pill-resistant. And it comes in over a dozen colors.

In addition to all the great solid colore options, J.Crew offers its cashmere crewnecks in marled and patterned styles for an additional $20.

J.Crew’s cashmere V-neck is made from the same great material as its crewnecks. I appreciated that the neckhole’s proportions are perfect for layering over a collared shirt. Sadly, even though V-necks are as big as they’ve ever been, this one only comes in ho-hum black, navy, and gray.

In addition to looking nice, this cable-knit cashmere is a bit thicker and warmer than its flat counterparts. It’s also more expensive. That said, it’s still a lot less than the similar Polo Ralph Lauren cashmere cable-knit. The Polo comes in more colors, but the J.Crew is the better value.

I loved the dry texture of this waffle-knit cashmere polo but ultimately preferred how it looked on the more casual, raglan-sleeve crewneck.

I’m not dogmatic about men’s clothing styles — I actually quite like J.Crew’s new line of cotton-collared wool rugby sweaters as a sort of two-great-tastes-that-taste-great-together mash-up — but adding a cable-knit pattern to the mix crosses into clothing design Mad Libs territory.

entry.title: The Best Water Fountains for Cats and Dogs, According to Vets and Behaviorists
entry.summary: According to vets, pet owners, and animal behaviorists.
entry.content:
This year we rescued Georgie, a basset-hound mix, and I noticed almost immediately that her long, scruffy fur — compared to our other basset hound, Ringo’s, short hair — made the water bowls look much dirtier. They both leave their fair share of food crumbs behind, so I decided to try a pet water fountain, which uses a motorized pump and a built-in filter to trap debris and keep water cleaner. “Some dogs are naturally more interested in running water and will drink more readily from a fountain than a traditional bowl,” says registered vet nurse Jessica Simms at Butternut Box. The same is true for cats, as my colleague Amelia Jerden learned from the cat experts she consulted. So if you have a busy household like mine or Amelia’s, where water bowls quickly collect hair, food pieces, or other debris, you might also consider a water fountain, since circulating water means a steady supply of fresh drinking water throughout the day.

When you first try a water fountain for your pet, Simms recommends keeping a normal water bowl available alongside it. “Dogs have their own preferences, and some will take to running water immediately, while others might be wary of the noise or movement,” she says. Jennifer Van de Kieft, a cat behaviorist and nutritionist for Cat Advocate, said that’s also true for cats: “Cats prefer to drink from multiple water sources away from their food dish,” she says, so a fountain and water bowl can ease the transition and provide variety. Because a fountain gets your pet to drink more, says Simms, “it can be particularly beneficial for reluctant drinkers, senior dogs, or dogs with a history of urinary tract issues or kidney conditions, where maintaining optimal hydration can form an important part of their nursing care plan.” (Just note: All the sources we spoke to told us that a sudden change in water intake, whether your pet is drinking significantly more or avoiding water, is worth discussing with your vet, as it can sometimes signal underlying health issues.)

Below, you’ll find water-fountain options for cats and dogs, from glass and ceramic ones to cordless and large-capacity picks.

Simms told me that first and foremost, you should choose a fountain that’s easy to clean. “A fountain only helps with hydration if the water stays fresh. If it isn’t cleaned regularly, bacterial biofilm can quickly build up, creating a slippery layer on the fountain’s surfaces,” Simms says. Owners should look for one that allows you to take the whole thing apart and clean the bowl, pump, and filter regularly. If you can’t commit to regular cleaning, you may be better off refilling a simple bowl every day, says cat-behavior consultant Dr. Mikel Delgado.

Stainless steel, glass, or ceramic are the best materials since they’re durable and straightforward to clean and resist bacteria buildup. Plastic bowls can also cause some pets to develop chin acne, says Kerrie McKeon, resident cat expert at the animal-welfare and adoption organization Bideawee, so even if the fountain has some plastic components, it’s a good idea to prioritize a nonplastic bowl. Unfortunately, like most small appliances for humans, water fountains for pets still include some amount of plastic, whether it’s the pumps, filters, or small connectors.

If you’re trying to avoid plastic bowls since they can harbor bacteria, the PetSafe Drinkwell 360 comes recommended by Dr. Ambika Vaid, an integrative veterinarian and the veterinary adviser to dog-food brand Badlands Ranch. “The stainless steel helps reduce the risk of chin acne and facial pustules that can occur with plastic bowls, and the fountain comes apart completely, making it easy to clean thoroughly,” Vaid says. This water fountain also uses dual-filtration technology thanks to a carbon filter and foam filter, which Vaid says is a great option for pets. “Activated carbon helps reduce unwanted odors and tastes, while the foam traps hair, dust, and other debris to help keep the water clean,” she says, adding that the most important thing is to ensure you are cleaning it thoroughly and properly to prevent bacterial overgrowth. “Just because the water is moving doesn’t mean that it cannot form bacteria,” Vaid told me. With a 128-ounce capacity (about one gallon), this also has a solid reservoir for your furry friend. “It is also important to offer fresh water daily and change the filters regularly.”

PetSafe recently launched this fountain, which has a 60-ounce water tank and is designed for small dogs and cats. I’ve been testing it with my two dogs, and while the reservoir is clearly not big enough based on how much I needed to refill it each night, the HydroSphere would work well for any smaller pet. I found the water flow to be incredibly quiet, a key attribute for any noise-sensitive pets. Water in the reservoir bubbles up onto a bowl made of food-grade stainless steel, though the tank underneath is plastic. It also has a plastic splash guard to keep water inside the bowl as they are slurping it up. Another feature I appreciated is the LED indicator panel, which will tell you when water levels are low or the filter needs to be changed. It will also automatically shut off when the water gets extremely low, preventing any annoying dripping sounds.

Deals editor Sam Daly recommends this raindrop-shaped stainless-steel fountain, which she purchased after getting tired of the maintenance required for a plastic fountain. In addition to it being easy to keep clean — Daly says she hand-washes the entire fountain once a month, though the top parts are dishwasher-safe — she also likes the fountain’s unique shape. “It doesn’t hurt that it’s the nicest-looking cat fountain I’ve seen on the market,” she says. “It makes me think of a fountain you might find in a garden.” Her cats also appreciate the raindrop design, which is wide and low enough that they don’t have to crane their necks. Daly thinks the rapidly flowing water, which is faster than her previous fountain, encourages her cats to drink more. With a 60-ounce capacity, this Pioneer Pet fountain is best-suited to cats and small dogs. Pioneer Pet also makes a 128-ounce fountain that may suit larger dogs, but it has a different design.

Jerden bought the Catit Pixi fountain shortly after adopting her two cats, when the vet suggested a fountain to entice them to drink after they became dehydrated while sick. The Pixi, which has a shallow bowl and 84-ounce capacity, is primarily made of plastic but has a stainless-steel drinking bowl. While she’d prefer an entirely stainless design, there’s plenty to like about the Pixi. The elevated shallow bowl is easy for her cats to drink from, and because the reservoir of water is covered by the stainless-steel bowl, they can’t splash in the water — something she often catches them doing with a simple bowl of water or fountain with an open reservoir. They also like to drink straight from the fountain, so she appreciates that this bowl provides multiple ways for them to drink. The indicator light on the front of the fountain (the “nose and whiskers”), which turns red if the water level is low inside the reservoir, is handy for the owner. And if you or your pets are sensitive to noise, you’ll be glad to know this one is nearly silent. Jerden rarely ever hears it running, even though it’s in a central area of her apartment. Like all fountains, it does require regular maintenance. Jerden’s husband wipes down the reservoir with vinegar to disinfect it and rinses out the bowl to keep the water fresh, in addition to changing the filters monthly.

If you’re part of a multi-dog household or own a very thirsty pet, consider this Petlibro water fountain, which can hold over two gallons of water. It’s the fountain I keep running in my own home since it doesn’t require constant refills compared to other fountains with smaller reservoirs. The transparent water tank has a refill line, which makes it simple to keep track of how much water it needs. I also keep it plugged into the outlet closest to our sink, so I can easily fill up a pitcher of water and pour it into the fountain.

I love that it clears debris quickly thanks to the filter having five heavy-duty layers: non-woven fabric, ion-exchange resin, activated carbon, silver ceramic balls, and a sponge, which help to trap water impurities, outdoor matter (like grass or leaves), and pet hair. It’s also designed to have a whirlpool-like flow, so everything is properly filtered down and doesn’t get stuck to the sides of the bowl. My dogs Ringo and Georgie took to it after only a few days, and I often see them choosing to drink from the Petlibro over their normal water bowls now. It’s been such a hit that even Benny, my family’s rather particular Great Dane, drank from the fountain during a dinner party. My parents now have one at their house for Benny and their Aussie mix, Shea. The main drawback is the BPA-free plastic construction — I’m still on the hunt for a large-capacity stainless-steel water fountain for my dogs. And note: The brand also recommends cleaning the fountain weekly and changing the filter biweekly.

If you want to avoid plastic, glass is another great option. Brook’s all-glass water fountain comes recommended by Delgado. She says that while it is more fragile than stainless steel or ceramic, it’s easy to keep clean and simple to replace parts, if needed — Brook sells spare parts for every component of the fountain. The Brook’s glass is lead-free, and the only non-glass components are the carbon filter and pump. When the water is flowing, you can choose between three flow rates (low, medium, and full). The Brook has a 90-ounce capacity, making it best suited for cats and small-to-medium dogs. You can also add on a stand and/or mat to help contain spillage, at an additional cost.

Jerden just started testing out the Brook with her two cats after hearing Delgado’s recommendation and can attest that it is relatively easy to put together and looks nice. Her cats have taken quickly to drinking from the spout, though they also enjoy splashing their paws in the water bowl and making a mess — something to consider if your cats are similarly mischievous.

Ceramic is easier to keep clean than plastic in the long term, and it looks a little homier than stainless steel. Van de Kieft used this ceramic fountain with her cats for many years. While she now prefers using a simple water bowl for the easier maintenance, Van de Kieft says that the Creekside is a good-quality fountain and that she found PetSafe’s customer service to be excellent when she needed a replacement part. The fountain has a similar design to the Brook, with a bubbler on top of an open bowl of water, and it has a pump and filter to keep the recirculating water clean. The ceramic components of the fountain are also top-rack dishwasher safe.

One of the most finicky aspects of setting up a water fountain for your pets is finding a convenient place to plug it in. For her cats, senior editor Winnie Yang uses PetLibro’s Dockstream fountain, which is completely cordless and operates on a rechargeable battery that lasts up to 30 days. Without needing to be plugged in, the PetLibro can be placed wherever is convenient in your home; you also don’t need to worry about your pet’s access to water during a power outage. Like my Pixi fountain, the Dockstream is primarily made of plastic with a stainless-steel bowl. Yang says, in retrospect, she might have chosen PetLibro’s stainless-steel model instead, though it’s not cordless like this model. The Dockstream has a spout that flows into a bowl, giving pets multiple ways to drink. When it’s not plugged in, the PetLibro uses radar detection to begin flowing when your pet walks by; it runs continually if you leave it plugged in. Yang notes the Dockstream does require frequent filter replacements (every two weeks). Her husband cleans the fountain weekly as well, though he says the internal pieces are well-designed to avoid any nooks and crannies where gunk can hide. And, of course, if you use it wirelessly, you’ll need to ensure it is charged.

Cats are drawn to flowing water, so it’s not uncommon for owners to find their feline friends drinking straight from the sink. For cats that look to the faucet for a drink, Delgado recommends the AquaPurr, which has been a successful recommendation for several of her cat-behavior clients. It’ll be a little more effort to set up than some of the other fountains on this list, as it hooks up to your sink. That means less maintenance long term, as you don’t need to change the water out. The AquaPur is motion-activated, so it will start flowing with water straight from the faucet when your cat wants a drink. It can be plugged in or run on batteries, so you can set it up at whichever sink is most convenient for you. There is also a remote control, which you can use to control the sensor’s range and the time range during which the faucet runs.

entry.title: What Skin-Care Brand Founder Indie Lee Buys at the Drugstore
entry.summary: “It’s like a spa vacation in your shower.”
entry.content:
Here at the Strategist, we love hearing about everyday stuff that actually works. That line of thinking extends to the drugstore — and even grocery store — beauty products in our medicine cabinets, shower caddies, and makeup bags. In our series “Beauty Aisle,” we talk to folks in the beauty industry — aestheticians, hairstylists, makeup artists, dermatologists, and the like — about the go-to affordable products they keep stocked. For this installment, Strategist beauty writer Krista Bennett DeMaio chatted with Indie Lee, founder of Indie Lee Skincare, about the products she loves at Whole Foods.

I’m obsessed with this brand. I love its bar soaps, bath soaks, and especially the shower steamer. It’s like a spa vacation in your shower. You put one on your shower floor and the eucalyptus or lavender becomes effervescent. Your shower smells so good. It’s a real aromatic treat.

This is what I use every day. It’s in my shower and on my vanity. It’s a gel cleanser you can use morning and night. It’ll remove all your makeup, but it’s not going to strip your skin. It contains blackberry extract, which is rich in polyphenols. It’s just fantastic. And it’s packaged in postconsumer recycled plastic. I designed this line for Whole Foods so people can explore Indie Lee without the higher price point.

When you choose body tools, always look for the natural elements because they’re going to end up in the garbage. Loofahs are actually a gourd — I grow them at my house. So this is a great option. It’s sustainable; it’s not going to sit in a landfill. Even if it’s not organic, at least you know it’s a vegetable base.

A classic. You can use this castile soap on anything. It does everything, and I love that it also comes as a bar soap. Dr. Bronner’s is a great brand, really committed to regenerative agriculture and stewardship of the earth, which means taking active responsibility to care for the earth — it’s a phenomenal, phenomenal brand.

This Australian brand has really great hand and bodywashes, but it also has fruit and vegetable washes that use essential oils for their fragrance. I love what Koala Eco is doing.

Mineral Fusion has great colors and staying power, in terms of chipping, and the polishes are clean.

It’s so important to look at what’s in your feminine-hygiene products. You are inserting some of these products into your body, so you really need to be mindful about their ingredients. Flo is a great product line made with organic bamboo.

My all-time favorite toothpaste, hands down, and it’s from a small brand. I love it because it doesn’t contain fluoride, which we don’t need to be ingesting. It’s great for enamel health and breath.

entry.summary: From André Leon Talley’s UGGs to Debi Mazar’s dish soap.
entry.content:
Our “What I Can’t Live Without” series started with a simple question: What are the everyday things that celebrities actually use and like? Not the red-carpet diamonds or the $6,000 cashmere throw blanket, but the mouthwashes, the ankle socks, the personal fans. In 2016, Common’s answer was Frank Ocean’s album Blonde, Billy Crudup’s was a Hammacher Schlemmer sound machine, and Rachel Antonoff’s was Blistex Lip Medex. Getting celebrities to respond wasn’t easy initially. “It was just us trying to convince people to do it in the beginning,” says New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff. But some, like Antonoff, were early gets. (“I don’t remember exactly how it was sold to me, but I love a recommendation,” says Antonoff. “I have this interior Rolodex of like, No, this is the best detergent.”) In the ten years since, we’ve interviewed hundreds of celebrities and notable people, from New York City mayoral candidates and the stars of the Real Housewives to Amy Sedaris and Jennifer Aniston. And the column has grown into one of our flagship series (and led to offshoots like “What I Can’t Cook Without” and “What My Kids Can’t Live Without”). Now, we’re looking back at ten of the most memorable “What I Can’t Live Without” columns by returning to the celebrities and writers who interviewed them.

Longtime contributing Vogue editor André Leon Talley, who died in 2022, was known for his high-end taste — he collected monogrammed Louis Vuitton suitcases and Limoges luncheon plates with drawings by Jean Cocteau — but his 2016 “What I Can’t Live Without,” the first in the series, was less the stuff of a Christie’s auction, and decidedly more down to earth. “He’s one of the most glamorous people in the world, and he’s talking about UGGs,” says Swerdloff of his list, which also included cleaning supplies and an electric toothbrush. It was that toothbrush that inspired the text that for years ran at the beginning of every column: If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what famous people add to their carts. Not the JAR brooch and Louis XV chair, but the hand sanitizer and the electric toothbrush.

If it wasn’t for Aubrey Plaza, we might not know about Real Purity’s natural deodorant. It turns out that Plaza, whose list was published in 2017, heard about it from Judy Greer, who later included it in her “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2022. “I do everything Judy Greer tells me to do,” said Plaza at the time. Strategist editors followed suit: Swerdloff and senior editor Simone Kitchens both still use the deodorant. Several other items from Plaza’s list have become Strategist canon, too: Writer Kitty Guo credits the Oribe Dry Texturizing Spray with saving her bad haircut, alongside Lucas Papaw “miracle ointment,” which has appeared in Dido’s, Erin Wasson’s, Selma Blair’s, and Alison Brie’s “What I Can’t Live Withouts” since.

Often, we only get a short amount of time to chat with celebrities about their items — but sometimes they can’t help but gab. What was meant to be a tightly scheduled 15-minute phone call between Debi Mazar and former writer Chloe Anello lasted more than two hours. “She knew who she was. She knew what she liked,” Anello says. “As we were talking about one thing, it reminded her of something else that she loved.” When Anello got off the phone, she had about 60-something items, 50 of which we ran in one of our longer columns in the series.

“I’m a person who tries things for people and gives my opinions. I’ve been given a lot of free stuff because of my job. They let me take home things that I discover on the set. I’m always flying through an airport and I’m like, Oh, what’s this?” says Mazar. When the list was published, “Everyone called me, like, ‘Oh, my God. I love this list. I am so ordering that.’” Five years later, she still wears Chanel No. 5 and agua de violetas, washes her dishes with Palmolive, and drinks Café Bustelo.

“I love the Strategist; I need the Strategist. So many of the things in my life I’ve gotten from the Strategist,” Jason Schwartzman told New York on a red carpet at Sundance in 2024. Months later, senior writer Lauren Ro met with him for his “What I Can’t Live Without” interview. Schwartzman showed Ro the phone case he got for his wife after reading Amelia Meath’s “What I Can’t Live Without” and a Pilot Varsity fountain pen he bought after reading Ottessa Moshfegh’s. The interview went on for nearly three hours over the course of two days, and the post became our most-viewed “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2024. Maybe it was thanks to his enthusiasm: for an airbrush he discovered on the set of Fargo, a light meter that was part of his research for Asteroid City, and Boggle Sit & Solve puzzles. “He’s somebody that loves to learn. You can just see that in the way that he has chosen the items and how he talks about them and how he has thought about using them,” says Ro.

When we talked to the My Year of Rest and Relaxation author in 2022, she was newly “pajamas obsessed” and sleeping in J.Crew’s End-on-End Cotton Long-Sleeved Pajama Set, a recent acquisition at the time. Moshfegh was wearing the very same pajamas when we called recently: “I didn’t sleep, therefore didn’t sleep in [them], but have been in my pajamas since last night and have not changed because I’m hopeful to sleep more,” she told us. It was the pair that she bought the same year as the interview, and even now, four years later, she still hears from people about them. “I would say every six months or so, somebody tells me that they wear the same pajamas as me,” says Moshfegh.

Similar to Debi Mazar’s multi-hour interview, Samantha Irby’s went from a quick hit to a two-hour call. In the first 40 minutes, she chatted about everything from scam texts to The Real Housewives of Miami. Then she got down to her stuff: There was her Owala (which later led to our investigation into the new status water bottle), the oregano oil a hippie recommended to her at a co-op, and the Lectrofan sound machine she credits with keeping her “marriage intact.” When we spoke to Irby again recently, she told us that she still reads the column and bought the incense Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee burns. “In the way that I’m curious about people, I assume people would be curious about me,” she says. “What does a person who has diarrhea all the time wipe their ass with? You need to know what the real shitters use.” (Charmin UltraStrong rolls, in Irby’s case.)

We’ve regularly talked to people with particular, exacting, and exceptional taste over the years — and there might be no better example than designer John Derian. He’s consistent, too: We interviewed Derian in 2017 and again in 2023 and learned that he still used every single thing on his original list, including the Zig Memory System Calligraphy Dual Tip Marker and Tom’s of Maine Unscented Deodorant. “I think probably the first time I was just sort of like, I’m so basic,” jokes Derian. Basic or not, it turns out that he’s in good company with his recommendations: Danny Meyer also seasons with Maldon sea-salt flakes; Ana Gastayer wears the same deodorant brand, Schmidt’s; and Kiehl’s Ultra Facial Moisturizer SPF 30 protects Chloe Bailey in the Caribbean sun.

No “What I Can’t Live Without” has the number of comments that 91-year-old former talk-show host Sally Jessy Raphael’s 2025 column does: 112, as of the publication of this article. (That’s even more than the 87 left for Ballerina Farm’s Hannah Neeleman and Diane von Furstenberg’s 71.) As one reader wrote, “This is the apotheosis of the ‘Can’t Live Without’ column.” Others loved her Coke Zero Cherry and Sharpie markers. Not that Raphael is reading the comments: “I don’t ever look and see what anyone thinks. I never watch a show I’ve done. People say, ‘Well, haven’t you seen any movie you’ve been in?’ The answer is no,” says Raphael.

When we talked to Lena Dunham in 2017 for the column, she had just wrapped Girls. Nine years later, as Dunham’s memoir Famesick was about to come out, we checked back in to hear about her eBay and Etsy search terms — which we ran in our Secret Strategist newsletter — and her latest batch of things she can’t live without. Her updated list included the Ozlo Sleepbuds she learned about from Susan Orlean’s “What I Can’t Live Without” (both go to bed listening to true-crime podcasts) and Four Thousand Weeks by Oliver Burkeman for “making choices about what’s important to you.” Readers took Dunham’s recommendations seriously; they were among the most-purchased items on the site this April. “I think Lena Dunham always knows what the hook is,” says Erin Schwartz, who spoke with Dunham over email, phone, and text. “Like the thing about all of her animals wanting to sit on the crystal infrared mat, I thought it was just such an indelible image of this sort of woo-woo mat and the rabbits flustered on it.”

“She really in so many ways, was humbly showing off that she has been on the forefront of a trend, with the Free City T-shirts being on Girlfriends and wearing Ruby Woo, for so long,” says senior writer Liza Corsillo of her call with Tracee Ellis Ross for the actress’s 2026 “What I Can’t Live Without.” Not long after, Corsillo got tickets to Tracee Ellis Ross’s Broadway show Every Brilliant Thing and she recognized Ross wearing a few things from her list, like the Levi’s 1950’s 701 jeans and Asics they talked about. Ross also told us she carried Alex Mill’s Perfect Weekend Tote (monogrammed with her initials, TER) to and from the theater as well. “It makes her feel like she’s part of the Strat family,” says Corsillo. (It was featured on the site as the perfect mom bag in 2025.)

entry.title: I Found the Minimum Viable Sock
entry.summary: Truly no-show.
entry.content:
Maybe it’s an Asian Mom thing, but I believe shoes — with the exception of sandals, heels, and dress shoes — should always be worn with socks. They help with rubbing and blister prevention, yes, but they also feel more hygienic. I would never go sockless with sneakers, which is just gross. (Alas, I must confess that I don’t wear socks with my Nike Air Rifts, a transgression I pay for dearly.) When I want the no-show look (millennial that I am), I pair teeny-tiny liners with, for example, Vans slip-ons and my strappy Marni neoprene sneakers and feel smug about my foot-health choices.

Until recently, I didn’t know that even tinier, do-they-even-qualify-as-socks socks existed. Browsing the Hue site, I found toe toppers and open-toe mule liners and socks specifically designed for loafers. I called in a few styles to see if they would, in fact, work with pumps and slides and other special-occasion shoes (and actually stay on).

The cotton toe toppers, which are regular socks that have been cut off mid-foot, were the most intriguing to me, but I couldn’t immediately find a use for them. They extended too far up to be hidden and also seemed a little counterproductive. When you’re wearing mules or backless shoes, your toes need to be a little sweaty to grip the footbed when you’re walking. Then I tried them in my Vans and I realized that they and other slip-on sneakers were the perfect use case for these socks. In fact, they worked better than my liners, which are a little too thin and occasionally slip off my heels.

The Perfectly Bare toe covers are even freakier. They’re sheer on top and have a padded sole with silicone grips. I tried them in my pointy mules but they still showed, and as I said above, the only way to wear mules is without socks. (For open-toe slides, Hue makes a version that are like fingerless gloves, but for your feet. They look bonkers. I sadly did not get a chance to try these.)

I also tried the Perfectly Bare version of my go-to cotton liners, and they were exactly what I needed for a night out. I wore them to dinner with my patent opera shoes, which are so incredibly gorgeous but unfortunately quite stiff (as is the case with all patent leather). I usually wear them sockless (or with tights when it’s cold), but since I hadn’t worn them in a couple of months, I wasn’t in the mood to risk blisters.

The liners are thin like tights and also slippery in that pleasing way, preventing any kind of friction within the shoe. They stayed on my feet all night, and the seam and the silicone heel grip didn’t dig or rub at all. I felt free. At home, I tried them with my ballet flats — which I normally wear without socks — and they worked beautifully with those, too. They add no bulk, keeping dainty shoes dainty and my bunioned feet happy. And when it’s time to go sockless, I’ll have built up enough goodwill with my feet that hopefully they will not mind.

entry.title: The Only Gift Guide for a 5-Year-Old You’ll Ever Need
entry.summary: Including lots of toys that are not only fun but will sneakily help them practice new skills.
entry.content:
At 5 years old, children are learning how to play in groups and what it means to cooperate — two skills they’ll use on a daily basis as they start kindergarten. They may still struggle with sharing a favorite toy or reaching a consensus on which game to play. But they’re starting to have a better handle on their emotions and learning how to work through problems and conflicts, says George Sachs, a child psychologist and founder of the Sachs Center in Manhattan. You may even overhear them practicing their conflict-resolution skills via their dolls or while pretending to be a veterinarian who specializes in dragons and unicorns.

Meanwhile, they are also learning to write letters and simple words like their name, “dog,” and “cat,” and they are likely incorporating them into the drawings they make, says Jeannette Corey, director of the Bank Street Family Center. But giving them opportunities to practice these skills doesn’t have to feel like school. There are tons of games, toys, and art supplies to support these milestones without them even knowing it. The 30+ gifts below have been recommended by pros like Sachs and Corey as well as toy buyers, trend experts, educators, and highly discerning parents. Several of them also recently made our list of toys that are expensive but worth it — which means, yes, that some of the best toys for 5-year-olds require a bit of an investment. But perhaps there’s some comfort in knowing that 5-year-olds are at an ideal age for playing creatively and getting as much payoff as possible out of a thoughtful toy-store splurge.

We’ve organized the list by price, so if you have a specific budget in mind, you can use the table of contents to skip right to that section. Otherwise, read all the way through for a full picture of what 5-year-olds are into.

Meanwhile, if you’re also shopping for kids in other age groups, we have gift guides for 1-year-olds, 2-year-olds, 3-year-olds, 4-year-olds, 6-year-olds, 7-year-olds, 8-year-olds, 9-year-olds, 10-year-olds, 11-year-olds, and 12-year-olds — plus the meticulously curated Strategist Toy Store, filled with all our greatest hits.

Updated on October 20, 2026 
These gift ideas have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

By age 5, children who have previously been obsessed with making mini-cupcakes and pizzas out of Play-Doh are skilled enough to make sculptures worth saving. Air-dry modeling clay is just as satisfying to squeeze and squish and will permanently harden after a few days. Tze Chun, founder of Uprise Art, recommended this 24-color set in our guide to the best art supplies for kids; it includes cutting tools, extra plastic to keep unfinished projects from drying out, and an idea book for making specific shapes. The brand also sells 7-ounce packs of six different solid colors in case your child needs enough blue for an entire ocean.

But that’s not to say there’s no place for Play-Doh in their lives, especially if it comes in a Barbie set that lets them create 3-D outfits for their dolls. Each of the sets in this recently released series comes with an 11-inch Barbie doll, a stand, a sheet of Play-Doh that looks like fabric, a clothing cutter, a fringe or ruffle roller tool, a stamper, and hair and hat molds. There are also additional pattern sets in hearts, bows, and gems.

According to Fjona Berisha, a sales associate at the NYC toy store Kidding Around, 5-year-olds and their parents both love these postcard-size Dover Little Activity Books, which have center pages full of stickers that kids can use to decorate the background scene printed on the inside cover. This one features an empty silver sundae dish they can fill with scoops of ice cream, fruit, gummy worms, sprinkles, and other toppings. There are also designs where they can decorate a pumpkin or fill a pet store with animals.

This dinosaur headlamp is featured in our guide to the best outdoor toys and works both for camping trips and as a fun (and hands-free) way to explore your own backyard at night.

According to Kelly Harris Smith, founder of Boston-based art center Minni, Ooly Chunkies tempera paint sticks are universal and great for every age but especially ideal for impatient kindergartners. “They dry quickly, are washable, and the artwork made from overlapping or blending colors is often surprisingly beautiful,” she says. They were also recommended to us by Natalie Ebel, co-founder of Backdrop, who tells us “they go on smooth and look almost like gouache.” The sticks are nontoxic and easy for little kids to hold. And for Halloween or everyday dress-up, Ooly has a similar set of body and face paint sticks called “Body Doodlers.”

Like basic wooden blocks, bouncy balls are a perfect open-ended toy, says Dr. Roberta Golinkoff, a professor of child psychology at the University of Delaware and author of Becoming Brilliant: What Science Tells Us About Raising Successful Children. Nerf’s Super High Bounce balls can soar up to 50 feet in the air and will inspire dozens of game possibilities. I also love Crocodile Creek’s textured rubber playground balls, which come in multiple sizes (four, five, and seven inches) and are available in lots of colorful patterns, from unicorns and mermaids to insects and outer space. Or, for a sportier option, this Franklin playground ball is a solid choice; it’s slightly larger and comes with its own air pump.

Spot It! is a palm-size matching game that challenges kids to find the two identical images between two cards before other players do. And since it can be played by up to eight people at a time, it’s a great family game to keep in your bag for restaurants and doctor’s office waiting rooms. This one is animal-themed, but the game also comes in a bunch of different variations, including camping, numbers, and licensed editions like Disney characters and Paw Patrol.

Perler Beads are great for honing the already advanced fine motor control of a 5-year-old, while also allowing for open-ended artistic creation — the rainbow colors can be put in endless combinations onto pegboards in all kinds of shapes. Once in place, adults can help kids fuse the beads together with an iron.

Kids go wild for stomp rockets — a fact well acknowledged by both Sachs and Strategist contributor Steven John, who saw his own son take to them as early as age 2. At that age, he was more of a spectator than a rocket launcher, though; by age 5, kids have the balance and strength to send a rocket skyward on their own, something they will do repeatedly.

KiwiCo sells a wide range of individual craft sets and STEM kits, but it’s most well known for its monthly subscription boxes, including one for the 3-to-6 age range. Each kit has hands-on maker and art projects that are perfectly suited to the rapidly developing mind of the kindergartner and early-elementary-school child. “This subscription fosters collaboration, problem-solving, and independence,” says Halley Loeb Rossler, a special-education teacher from Tulsa, Oklahoma. Rossler notes that in her own home, her boys look forward to the delivery of their boxes every month.

Each of the characters in this series of mix-and-match Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle action figures has removable arms, legs, and heads that you can swap for the body parts of others — Leonardo’s head on Donatello’s body, for example — to delightfully Frankensteinian effect.

Golinkoff likes how walkie-talkies encourage collaboration, communication, and creativity. And Dr. Alexandra Figueras-Daniel, an assistant research professor at the National Institute for Early Education Research, is a fan because they encourage turn-taking and are a really fun way to practice and develop language and communication skills. This high-quality pair has three different channels, allowing for multiple lines of communication and a range of nearly two miles, making them ideal for use all over the neighborhood or even during visits to the zoo or amusement park (the quiet-crisp audio quality is especially helpful in such noisy environments).

Plus Plus — which have won all kinds of awards and develop engineering, design, and fine motor skills — are a favorite building toy of Strategist contributor Youngna Park and her two children, who at ages 7 and 9 are on the older end of the toy’s age range but still love playing with them. Each piece is exactly the same shape, like two plus signs stuck together, but the creative possibilities are endless. My husband works at a private school in Brooklyn where his summer-camp students were using this set of Plus Plus pieces to make Beyblade dupes that actually spin. That’s probably too advanced of a project for a 5-year-old, but kids can use Plus Plus to build much simpler things, too, and age 5 is a good time to introduce them.

With this kit, kids can build a variety of wacky robots and then actually watch them move, explains Laurie Schacht, chief toy officer of The Toy Insider. A step-by-step storybook manual (reading is required) follows Ty and Karlie, two young engineers, as they help fix the robots at the robot factory. The manual makes everything manageable with minimal adult assistance required. After assembling the LEGO-like blocks, kids will connect their structure to a ready-made motor.

Ebel recommends these colored pencils, which her 5-year-old loves because they are so “soft” and easy to draw with. “Nothing is more frustrating than a colored pencil that doesn’t really work,” Ebel says, “but these Prismacolor ones go on so smoothly,” making them a great gift for budding illustrators.

Maileg toys have a devoted following — and though they can be quite pricey, they are made to last. There is an entire mouse universe including dollhouses, vehicles, furniture, lots and lots of mice, and even a pumpkin carriage on wheels.

As kids get more confident in their gross motor skills, they also risk falling and hurting themselves on the monkey bars or other playground equipment. Thus, at any given time in elementary school, there usually are at least a couple children with an arm or a leg in a cast. When Calavan heard that her Milk Teeth co-founder Catherine Newell-Hanson’s then 5-year-old daughter had broken her arm, Calavan ordered a stuffy with a matching cast as a gift. “My son and I picked the animal, which body part to put the cast on, and the color of the cast,” says Calavan, adding that the gift was a huge hit. “She was so excited and we were sitting outside at a pizza restaurant when she opened it, and all the other diners lost their minds over how cute it was. Then she brought it into school the next day.”

The original Gravitrax modular marble run is in our guide to the best gifts for 7-year-olds, with a note that it’s a bit of a challenge for that age. Gravitrax Junior pieces are sized for smaller hands and designed for beginners. Berisha says these sets are really cool and fun for kids of mixed ages to work on together. Compared to the set designed for older kids, this one is easier to assemble and available in a few different themes: jungle, arctic, desert, and ocean. Each box comes with multiple possible track layouts as well as baseplates, marbles, a bridge, slopes, curves, a seesaw, cardboard animals, and 3-D themed decorative elements.

Swiss brand Caran D’Ache is also known for its high-quality art supplies. This kid-focused travel kit comes with a set of watercolor pencils, a set of watercolor pastels, a reservoir brush for mess-free painting on the go, travel-themed stickers, a carrying case, and a dozen postcards with line drawings you can color in.

Magna-Tiles have been recommended by almost every parent and development expert we’ve talked to in the last few years. That’s because they support a wide range of developmental skills, keep kids engaged in independent play, and are fun for the whole family. We included the basic starter set of Magna-Tiles in our gift guide for 3-year-olds. And while growing a collection gets pricey quick, the many different styles available help add a ton of play value. For more enthusiastic builders and kids who love things with wheels, consider a set of downhill roads and cars, the newly released Rail Racers set that turns basic tiles into ball ramps, or the XL construction set with a dump truck and working crane.

In addition to Magna-Tiles, Lizzie Assa, founder of the Workspace for Children and mother of three, highlighted the Australian brand Connetix as one of her personal favorite magnetic building toys, noting that many of the different brands are compatible with each other. Like Magna-Tiles, Connetix makes a wide range of basic sets in bright rainbow colors, pastels, and clear (perfect for an icy Elsa build). It also makes themed sets, including a transportation pack with wheeled bases that can be linked from end to end, have real rubber tires, and work as a chassis for cars, trucks, boats, or trains.

For New York Magazine features writer and mom of two Kathryn VanArendonk, the Yoto Mini, a kid-friendly audio player, is one of a few kids’ essentials she would immediately repurchase if it got lost or somehow destroyed. In VanArendonk’s eyes, the Yoto is a superior choice for older kids compared to the younger-skewing Toniebox, because the cards can hold longer tracks of audio, including chapter books and whole albums, and it lets you easily skip around from track to track. She also loves how much freedom it gives her kids to listen to the books and podcasts they like.

There’s also a “full-size” Yoto player that offers all the same features as the more portable Mini, for families who want to use it as more of a “keep it on the nightstand” device. The full-size Yoto has a nightlight and room thermometer and promises a longer battery life, better sound quality, and wireless charging capability. Both the Mini and the full-size Yoto players have an alarm-clock function, too.

Read more: Which Is Better, the Yoto Mini or the Toniebox?

“Dramatic play at this age can be more sophisticated,” says Figueras-Daniel, who adds that “having detailed accessories” — like those in this Playmobil animal hotel — adds to the play. The set has an outdoor pen and a bathtub for dogs on one side and a kitty lounge area on the other. There are also amenities for other pets like hamsters and birds — in other words, everything a 5-year-old might need to recreate a true-to-life scene. The attention to detail, and the vast array of other Playmobil sets you can use in concert with this one, makes it engaging for friends, parents, and caregivers too.

For 5-year-olds who are obsessed with tweens and teens, like my rising kindergartner niece, here’s an intricately designed classroom play set from Our Generation, a doll brand that’s mostly found at Target. The set features lockers outside the classroom door and a real working clock, fire alarm, school bell, and lights, plus accessories and school supplies. And while it’s built for Our Generation dolls, it’s compatible with other 18-inch dolls like Zoe, above, or American Girl Dolls.

One of the most essential toys for any kid is a scooter, and Carrie Wren of Two Wheeling Tots agrees with most of the parents and experts we have talked to that Micro Kickboard makes the best scooters on the market. “Their attention to detail, quality of design, and precision of build just can’t be beat,” she says. “No one really comes close, even though everyone tries to copy them.” The brand’s scooters are known for being lightweight and easy to use for toddlers all the way up to tweens. This one is designed for kids from roughly 5 to 12 years old and can support up to 110 pounds. Plus the handlebars are adjustable so it can grow with your child. Note that this scooter also comes in a Mini size that is rated for kids from 2 to 5, if your child is on the smaller side (and this wonderfully thorough guide from the brand can help you determine which size to choose).

A classic wooden-train set will keep most kids busy for hours and may ultimately hold a top spot in their toy rotation for years. Artist Aaron Luckman and his wife, Birgit Wurster, who are parents to a rising first-grader, recommend splurging on a starter set from Brio and then adding less-expensive, compatible pieces from Ikea and Melissa & Doug. This cargo railway set comes with a handy storage bin, a battery-powered engine, three cranes, a truck, a bridge, mountainous rocks, and a crossing signal.

If you’ve got a kid who never tires of fort-making, you might be ready for Super Space magnetic building panels. They’re basically life-size Magna-Tiles that kids can use to build playhouses, spaceships, and lots more. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio has a set at home that she and her two daughters love playing with. Though they are great for a variety of ages, Trolio suggests 5 or 6 as a good starting point, because by then kids are a little bigger and more capable of building larger structures with them. They are also super-compact when stacked neatly, and thus very easy to store in a corner or under a couch.
